# Sourdough Starter and Bread

## About Sourdough

Sourdough bread is leavened by a live culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria rather than
commercial packaged yeast. The starter is a fermented mixture of flour and water that captures
and cultivates these naturally occurring microorganisms from the environment.

## Creating a Starter

Mix equal weights of whole wheat or rye flour with unchlorinated water in a clean jar.
Store at room temperature around 70 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Discard half the mixture and
feed with fresh flour and water every 12 to 24 hours. After five to seven days the culture
should be reliably active, doubling in size within four to six hours of feeding.

## Signs of a Healthy Starter

A healthy starter has a pleasant sour or yogurt-like aroma. It bubbles actively after feedings
and passes the float test: a spoonful dropped into water floats when the culture is at peak activity.
Hooch, a dark liquid layer, indicates the starter is hungry and needs feeding sooner.

## Bulk Fermentation

Once the starter is active, combine it with flour, water, and salt to make the dough.
Bulk fermentation at room temperature takes four to eight hours depending on temperature.
Perform stretch-and-fold cycles every 30 minutes for the first two hours to develop gluten strength.

## Cold Proofing and Baking

Shape the dough and place it in a floured banneton. Refrigerate overnight for eight to twelve hours
of cold retard proofing. Bake in a preheated Dutch oven at 500 degrees Fahrenheit with the lid on
for 20 minutes to trap steam, then remove the lid and bake another 20 to 25 minutes for a dark
caramelized crust.
